patches.name: Format Number
patches.summary: Turns a number into display text with set decimals, separators, a percent or K/M style, and your own prefix and suffix.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Format Number turns a number into text you can show in a Text layer, like a price, a score, or a like count.

- **Value** is the number to show.
- **Style** writes it as plain digits, as a percentage, or shortened: **Compact** turns 12,345 into 12K.
- **Decimals** sets how many digits follow the decimal point. The number rounds to fit.
- **Prefix** and **Suffix** add text around the number, such as "$" or " of 5". Include any spaces you want.
- **Group Thousands** adds separators: 12,500 instead of 12500.

Advanced ports control rounding, trailing zeros, leading zeros, and the separator characters (1.234,5 in many European languages).

## Tips
- For follower counts, use Compact with Decimals 1 and Trailing Zeros off: 1,200 shows 1.2K and 1,000 shows 1K.
- Countdowns read better with Rounding set to Up, so the label shows 1 until the last second is over.
- To join several values into one label, use Add set to Text.

## Coming from Origami
Origami has no number formatter. Format Number replaces labels built with Add set to Text or with a JavaScript patch.

inputs.description: The number to show as text.

enumOptions.name: Percent
enumOptions.description: Multiplies by 100 and adds %, so 0.42 shows 42%.

enumOptions.description: Shortens large numbers with K, M, B, and T, like 12.3K.

inputs.description: How the number is written: plain digits, a percentage, or shortened with K, M, B, and T.

inputs.name: Decimals
inputs.description: How many digits to show after the decimal point, from 0 to 20. With Compact, they apply to the shortened number (1.2K has 1).

inputs.name: Prefix
inputs.description: Text placed before the number, such as "$" or "Page ".

inputs.name: Suffix
inputs.description: Text placed after the number, such as " pts" or " of 5".

inputs.name: Group Thousands
inputs.description: When on, separates thousands (12,500); when off, shows 12500.

inputs.name: Trailing Zeros
inputs.description: When on, always shows every decimal place (12.50); when off, drops zeros at the end (12.5).

inputs.name: Rounding

enumOptions.name: Nearest
enumOptions.description: Rounds to the closest value; halves round away from zero, so 2.5 shows 3.

enumOptions.name: Down
enumOptions.description: Rounds toward negative infinity, so 2.9 shows 2 and −2.1 shows −3.

enumOptions.name: Up
enumOptions.description: Rounds toward positive infinity, so 2.1 shows 3.

inputs.description: How extra decimal places are rounded away.

inputs.name: Minimum Digits
inputs.description: Pads the whole-number part with leading zeros to at least this many digits: 2 shows 7 as 07.

inputs.name: Separators
inputs.description: Which characters separate thousands and decimals.

outputs.name: Text
outputs.description: The formatted number, including Prefix and Suffix.

commonMistakes: Percent shows 4200% instead of 42%: Percent multiplies by 100 because progress runs from 0 to 1. Feed it 0.42, or use Number with a Suffix of "%" when your value already runs from 0 to 100.
A price shows 12.5 instead of 12.50: Trailing Zeros is off. Turn it on so every decimal place shows.
The label shows 1234.567891: the number goes straight into the Text layer. Wire it through Format Number with Decimals set first.

patches.name: Text Length
patches.summary: Counts the characters in text, counting each emoji or accented letter as one character.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text Length counts the characters in **Text** and outputs the count as **Length**.

- Every character counts as 1, including spaces, punctuation, and line breaks.
- An emoji counts as 1, even skin-tone and flag emoji built from several parts, and so does an accented letter.
- Empty text has a length of 0.

## Tips
- A number wired into an on/off port, such as a layer's Enabled, is on while it's above 0. Wire Length there to show something only when the text isn't empty.
- For a character limit, compare Length with the limit using Greater Than, and turn a counter red when it's over.
- Substring counts characters the same way, so positions from one line up with the other.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper: `graphemes(s)` splits text into user-perceived characters (extended grapheme clusters): `Array.from(segmenter.segment(s), (x) => x.segment)` with one module-level `segmenter = new Intl.Segmenter(undefined, { granularity: "grapheme" })`. Grapheme boundaries don't depend on the locale. Where `Intl.Segmenter` is missing, fall back to code points (`Array.from(s)`) and log one warning per restart through `ctx.services.log("warn", …)`.

Each frame:
```
ctx.output("length", graphemes(ctx.input<string>("text")).length);
```

- Counting: "héllo" is 5 whether é is one code point or e plus a combining accent. "👍🏽", "🇯🇵", and "👩‍👩‍👧" are 1 each. "\r\n" is 1, and "" is 0. JavaScript's `string.length` (UTF-16 code units) is never used.
- Coercion: the `text` port converts values before evaluation (ARCHITECTURE.md §4). 3.5 becomes "3.5" (3), true becomes "true" (4), and 1/3 becomes "0.333333" (8).
- No trimming: leading and trailing spaces count.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; a loop of texts gives a loop of lengths.
- Performance: segmentation is O(n). Implementations may memoize the last text and result per loop index so long text isn't re-segmented every frame while it's unchanged.
- Frame 0: no special case.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: matches Origami's counting since its v73 emoji fix. Origami leaves the output unnamed; Sonobe calls it Length.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to count.

outputs.name: Length
outputs.description: How many characters Text has. Spaces, punctuation, and line breaks count, and each emoji counts as 1.

commonMistakes: Length never changes: the text is typed into the inspector, so it's a fixed value. Wire the text that changes into Text.
Length is one more than you expect: a trailing space or line break counts as a character. Remove it from the source, or check what the text holds with Watch.

examples.title: Type out a message letter by letter
examples.description: Wait's progress runs from 0 to 1 over 2 seconds, Transition scales it to the message's length, and Substring shows that many characters.
examples.outline:
layer message text "Message" @24,120 text←typed.output
patch launch whenPrototypeStarts
patch message_text textReplace text="Hi {name}, your order is on its way." find="{name}" replace="Sam"
patch message_length textLength text←message_text.output
patch reveal wait start←launch.started duration=2
patch shown transition<number> progress←reveal.progress start=0 end←message_length.length
patch typed substring text←message_text.output length←shown.output

patches.name: Split Text
patches.summary: Splits text into a loop of parts wherever a separator appears, like turning "Home,Search,Profile" into three tab labels.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Split Text cuts **Text** apart wherever **Token** appears and outputs the pieces as a loop: a list of values that makes a layer repeat once per item.

- **Token** is the separator, such as a comma, a space, or a line break. It must match exactly, including capital letters, and it isn't included in the parts.
- **Parts** is the loop of pieces, in order. When Token doesn't appear, Parts holds the whole text as one item.
- **Count** is how many parts there are.
- An empty Token splits the text into single characters, which is handy for animating letter by letter.
- Two tokens in a row leave an empty part between them. Turn on the advanced **Skip Empty** port to drop empty parts.

## Tips
- Wire Parts into a Text layer inside a group with Layout set to Row or Column to get one label per part.
- Feed Count into a Loop patch to get an index for staggering animations.
- A loop of texts splits each one and joins all the parts into one loop.

## Coming from Origami
The output is named Parts, and Count and Skip Empty are new. An empty Token splits into characters instead of returning the whole text.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to split. A loop of texts splits each one and joins all the parts into one loop.

inputs.name: Token
inputs.description: The separator to split at, such as "," or " "; it's left out of the parts. Leave it empty to split into single characters.

inputs.name: Skip Empty
inputs.description: When on, drops empty parts, such as the one between two commas in a row or after a trailing comma.

outputs.name: Parts
outputs.description: A loop of the pieces between separators, in order. When Token doesn't appear, it holds the whole text as one item.

commonMistakes: Every label after the first starts with a space: the text has a space after each comma, but Token is only ",". Set Token to ", ".
Only one item appears: Token doesn't appear in the text, or its capital letters differ. Make Token match the separator exactly.
The copies stack on top of each other: each part makes its own copy of the layer at the same position. Put the layer in a group with Layout set to Row or Column.

examples.title: Tab labels from one line of text
examples.outline:
layer tab_bar group "Tab Bar" @0,780 390x64 layout=row spacingMode=evenly
  layer tab_label text "Tab Label" text←labels.parts
patch labels splitText text="Home,Search,Inbox,Profile"

examples.title: Reveal a sentence word by word
examples.description: Loop turns Count into an index for each word, and Transition gives each word a later start: 0.3 s, 0.45 s, 0.6 s, and so on.
examples.outline:
layer sentence group "Sentence" @24,200 342x40 layout=row spacing=6
  layer word text "Word" text←words.parts opacity←fade.output
patch words splitText text="Make something people love" token=" "

patch stagger transition<number> progress←word_index.index start=0.3 end=0.45

patches.name: Text Starts With
patches.summary: Checks whether text begins with a given prefix, such as a slash command or https://.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text Starts With outputs **Starts With**: true when **Text** begins with **Prefix**, and false otherwise.

- It checks the very first characters, so a leading space counts: " hello" doesn't start with "hello".
- **Case Sensitive** is off by default, so "Hello" starts with "he". Turn it on when capitals matter.
- An empty Prefix always matches.

## Tips
- Wire Starts With into Option Picker's Option to choose between two colors or icons.
- For type-ahead search, feed a loop of names into Text and the search text into Prefix, then keep the matches with Loop Filter.
- Need a match anywhere in the text? Use Text Contains.

## Coming from Origami
Origami's version always matches capitals exactly and has no Case Sensitive port. Imported patches turn Case Sensitive on to keep that behavior.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper: `escapeRegExp(s) = s.replace(/[\\^$.*+?()[\]{}|\/]/g, "\\$&")`, which stays valid with the `u` flag.

Each frame:
```
const text = ctx.input<string>("text").normalize("NFC");
const prefix = ctx.input<string>("prefix").normalize("NFC");
const startsWith = ctx.input<boolean>("caseSensitive")
  ? text.startsWith(prefix)
  : new RegExp("^" + escapeRegExp(prefix), "iu").test(text);
ctx.output("startsWith", startsWith);
```

- Case: with Case Sensitive off, matching uses Unicode simple case folding (the `i` and `u` regex flags) and doesn't depend on the locale. "École" starts with "é", but "ß" doesn't match "SS". Cache compiled regexes by prefix.
- Normalization: both inputs are NFC-normalized, so composed and decomposed accents match.
- Edge cases: an empty Prefix gives true for any Text, including empty Text. A Prefix longer than Text gives false. Nothing is trimmed.
- Output: a state, not a pulse. It stays true while the condition holds, and pulse inputs downstream fire once when it turns true.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; Text, Prefix, and Case Sensitive may each be loops.
- Muted: outputs false.
- Frame 0: no special case.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Text Starts With (`builtin.textprefix`) has no Case Sensitive port and matches exactly, so importers set `caseSensitive: true` on imported patches. Origami doesn't document the empty-prefix result; Sonobe returns true. Origami leaves the output unnamed.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to check.

inputs.name: Prefix
inputs.description: The text that might appear at the very start of Text. An empty Prefix always matches.

inputs.name: Case Sensitive
inputs.description: When on, capital letters must match exactly; when off, case is ignored, so "Hello" starts with "he".

outputs.name: Starts With
outputs.description: True while Text begins with Prefix.

commonMistakes: A match is missed: the text starts with a space or line break, which counts. Remove it at the source, or use Text Contains when the position doesn't matter.
Everything matches while the search is empty: an empty Prefix always matches. Use Text Length to check that the search text isn't empty when nothing should match.

patches.name: Text Ends With
patches.summary: Checks whether text ends with a given suffix, such as a file extension or a question mark.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text Ends With outputs **Ends With**: true when **Text** finishes with **Suffix**, and false otherwise.

- It checks the very last characters, so a trailing space or line break counts: "hello " doesn't end with "hello".
- **Case Sensitive** is off by default, so "clip.MP4" ends with ".mp4". Turn it on when capitals matter.
- An empty Suffix always matches.

## Tips
- Check file types by extension: ".mp4" for videos, ".png" for images.
- Wire Ends With into a layer's Enabled to show a badge only when the text matches.
- Need a match anywhere in the text? Use Text Contains.

## Coming from Origami
Origami's version always matches capitals exactly and has no Case Sensitive port. Imported patches turn Case Sensitive on to keep that behavior.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helper: `escapeRegExp(s) = s.replace(/[\\^$.*+?()[\]{}|\/]/g, "\\$&")`, which stays valid with the `u` flag.

Each frame:
```
const text = ctx.input<string>("text").normalize("NFC");
const suffix = ctx.input<string>("suffix").normalize("NFC");
const endsWith = ctx.input<boolean>("caseSensitive")
  ? text.endsWith(suffix)
  : new RegExp(escapeRegExp(suffix) + "$", "iu").test(text);
ctx.output("endsWith", endsWith);
```

- Case: with Case Sensitive off, matching uses Unicode simple case folding (the `i` and `u` regex flags) and doesn't depend on the locale. Cache compiled regexes by suffix.
- Anchoring: without the `m` flag, `$` matches only at the very end, never before a trailing line break, so "hi\n" doesn't end with "hi".
- Normalization: both inputs are NFC-normalized, so composed and decomposed accents match.
- Edge cases: an empty Suffix gives true for any Text, including empty Text. A Suffix longer than Text gives false. Nothing is trimmed.
- Output: a state, not a pulse. It stays true while the condition holds.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; Text, Suffix, and Case Sensitive may each be loops.
- Muted: outputs false.
- Frame 0: no special case.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Text Ends With (`builtin.textsuffix`) has no Case Sensitive port and matches exactly, so importers set `caseSensitive: true` on imported patches. Origami doesn't document the empty-suffix result; Sonobe returns true. Origami leaves the output unnamed.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to check.

inputs.name: Suffix
inputs.description: The text that might appear at the very end of Text. An empty Suffix always matches.

inputs.name: Case Sensitive
inputs.description: When on, capital letters must match exactly; when off, case is ignored, so "clip.MP4" ends with ".mp4".

outputs.name: Ends With
outputs.description: True while Text finishes with Suffix.

commonMistakes: A match is missed: the text ends with a space or line break, which counts. Remove it at the source, or use Text Contains when the position doesn't matter.
"photo.jpeg" isn't treated as an image: the patch checks one Suffix, such as ".jpg". Use one Text Ends With per extension and combine them with Or.

patches.name: Text Contains
patches.summary: Checks whether text includes a search term anywhere and where the first match starts, for search filters and keyword checks.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text Contains looks for **Find** anywhere inside **Text**.

- **Contains** is true when Find appears at least once.
- **Index** is where the first match begins, counted in characters from 0: in "Hello world", "world" begins at 6. It's −1 when there's no match.
- **Case Sensitive** is off by default, so "Maya" contains "ma". Turn it on when capitals matter.
- An empty Find always matches with Index 0, so a search filter shows every item until someone types.

## Tips
- Build a search filter: feed a loop of names into Text and the search text into Find, then keep the items where Contains is true with Loop Filter.
- To dim rows that don't match instead of hiding them, wire Contains into an Option Picker set to Number and use its output as Opacity.
- Index counts characters the same way as Substring, so you can cut text at a match.

## Coming from Origami
Origami only has Text Starts With and Text Ends With. Text Contains matches anywhere in the text.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helpers:
- `escapeRegExp(s) = s.replace(/[\\^$.*+?()[\]{}|\/]/g, "\\$&")`, which stays valid with the `u` flag.
- `graphemeIndex(text, offset)`: the number of grapheme segments (`Intl.Segmenter`, granularity `"grapheme"`) that end at or before the UTF-16 `offset`, that is `segments.filter((s) => s.index + s.segment.length <= offset).length`. A match that begins inside a grapheme reports that grapheme's index.

Each frame:
```
const text = ctx.input<string>("text").normalize("NFC");
const find = ctx.input<string>("find").normalize("NFC");
const offset = ctx.input<boolean>("caseSensitive")
  ? text.indexOf(find)
  : text.search(new RegExp(escapeRegExp(find), "iu"));
ctx.output("contains", offset >= 0);
ctx.output("index", offset >= 0 ? graphemeIndex(text, offset) : -1);
```

- Case: with Case Sensitive off, matching uses Unicode simple case folding (the `i` and `u` regex flags) and doesn't depend on the locale. Cache compiled regexes by Find.
- Normalization: both inputs are NFC-normalized. Index counts graphemes of the normalized text, the same unit Text Length and Substring use.
- Edge cases: an empty Find gives Contains true and Index 0, even for empty Text. A Find longer than Text gives false and −1. Only the first match is reported.
- Examples: Text "Hello world" with Find "O" gives Contains true, Index 4. Text "👋🏽 hi" with Find "hi" gives Index 2.
- Output: Contains is a state, not a pulse.
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; Text, Find, and Case Sensitive may each be loops.
- Muted: outputs Contains false and Index −1.
- Frame 0: no special case.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Sonobe-native (CONVENTIONS.md §18.1). Origami only has starts-with and ends-with checks.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to search in.

inputs.name: Find
inputs.description: The text to look for anywhere in Text. An empty Find always matches.

inputs.name: Case Sensitive
inputs.description: When on, capital letters must match exactly; when off, case is ignored, so "Maya" contains "ma".

outputs.name: Contains
outputs.description: True while Find appears somewhere in Text.

outputs.name: Index
outputs.description: Where the first match begins, counted in characters from 0, or −1 when there's no match.

commonMistakes: Every item matches before anyone types: an empty Find always matches. That's usually right for a search filter; otherwise, also require that the search text's Text Length is above 0.
"cafe" doesn't find "café": accented letters are different letters. Search with the accent, or replace accented letters in both texts with Text Replace first.

patches.name: Text Replace
patches.summary: Replaces every occurrence of some text with other text, for templates like "Hi {name}" or removing characters.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Text Replace searches **Text** for **Find** and puts **Replace** in place of every match.

- Matches are found left to right and never overlap: replacing "aa" in "aaa" makes one replacement.
- **Replace** can be empty, which deletes every match.
- **Case Sensitive** is off by default, so Find "hi" also replaces "Hi". Turn it on to replace only exact capitals.
- Find is plain text, not a pattern: characters like $ and * match themselves.
- An empty Find leaves the text unchanged.

## Tips
- Write templates with placeholders such as {name}, then fill each placeholder with its own Text Replace.
- Chain patches to replace several things, such as removing both spaces and dashes from a phone number.
- Use Change Case after it when the result needs consistent capitals.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to search.

inputs.name: Find
inputs.description: The text to look for. Every match is replaced, and an empty Find changes nothing.

inputs.name: Replace
inputs.description: The text that takes each match's place. Leave it empty to delete the matches.

inputs.name: Case Sensitive
inputs.description: When on, capital letters must match exactly; when off, case is ignored, so Find "hi" also replaces "Hi" and "HI".

outputs.name: Output
outputs.description: Text with every match of Find replaced.

commonMistakes: Only one placeholder gets filled: one Text Replace fills one placeholder. Chain a second patch for {date}, wiring the first Output into its Text.
Parts of other words change too: Find matches inside words, so "art" also changes "start". Include the spaces around the word in both Find and Replace.

patches.name: Change Case
patches.summary: Changes text to uppercase, lowercase, capitalized words, or sentence case.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Change Case rewrites the capital letters in **Text** and outputs the result.

- **Uppercase** makes every letter a capital: "RECENTLY PLAYED".
- **Lowercase** makes every letter small: "recently played".
- **Capitalize Words** capitalizes the first letter of each word and lowercases the rest: "Recently Played".
- **Sentence Case** capitalizes the first letter of each sentence and lowercases the rest: "Recently played".

Characters without capitals, such as digits, emoji, and punctuation, stay the same.

## Tips
- To compare typed text with a known answer, lowercase both sides first.
- When you only need the look on screen, set the Text layer's Transform property instead. Use Change Case when you need the changed text itself, to compare it or send it somewhere.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly Text Transform. The Transform port is named Case, Capitalized is named Capitalize Words, and Sentence Case is new.

inputs.description: The text to change.

patches.name: Substring
patches.summary: Keeps part of some text, a number of characters from a starting position, for initials, previews, and shortened titles.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Substring keeps a stretch of **Text** and drops the rest.

- **Start** is the character to begin at, counted from 0, so 0 is the first character.
- **Length** is how many characters to keep. Asking for more than remain keeps everything to the end.
- **Ellipsis** adds "…" at the end when characters after the kept part were cut off.
- Emoji and accented letters count as one character, the same as in Text Length.

For example, Text "Saturday" with Start 0 and Length 3 gives "Sat".

## Tips
- For initials, use Length 1 on a first name and a last name, then join them with Add set to Text.
- To shorten how a Text layer looks on screen, set its Max Lines property instead. Use Substring when you need the shortened text itself.
- Animate Length from 0 up to the text's length for a typewriter effect.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly Trim Text. Position is named Start, and Ellipsis is new.
patches.behavior:
Stateless.

Helpers: `graphemes(s)` as in textLength, and `whole(x) = Number.isFinite(x) ? Math.floor(x + 1e-6) : 0`.

Each frame:
```
const chars = graphemes(ctx.input<string>("text"));
const start = whole(ctx.input<number>("start")); // the index port already delivers an integer ≥ 0
const length = Math.max(0, whole(ctx.input<number>("length")));
const end = Math.min(chars.length, start + length);
let output = start < chars.length ? chars.slice(start, end).join("") : "";
if (ctx.input<boolean>("ellipsis") && output !== "" && end < chars.length) output = output.trimEnd() + "…";
ctx.output("output", output);
```

- Units: user-perceived characters (grapheme clusters), so slicing never splits an emoji or separates an accent from its letter.
- Ranges (CONVENTIONS.md §18.5.9): negative values never count from the end. Start arrives through the index port clamped to at least 0, and a negative Length counts as 0. Fractions round down after a 1e-6 epsilon, so an animated 2.9999999 keeps 3 characters.
- Ellipsis: "…" is U+2026, one character. Whitespace before it is trimmed, so "Weekend hiking " plus the ellipsis gives "Weekend hiking…". Nothing is added when the output is empty or already reaches the end. The ellipsis is extra: Length 10 with Ellipsis on gives up to 11 characters.
- Examples: "Saturday" with Start 3 and Length 3 gives "urd". Start 8 gives "". "👋🏽 hi" with Start 0 and Length 1 gives "👋🏽".
- Loops: evaluates once per loop index; Text, Start, Length, and Ellipsis may each be loops.
- Edge cases: empty Text gives "". A non-finite Start or Length counts as 0.
- Frame 0: no special case.
- Restart and dispose: nothing to reset or release.
- Coming from Origami: Trim Text (`builtin.textsubstring`), with ports Text, Position, and Length. Origami doesn't document zero-based counting or out-of-range handling; Sonobe counts from 0 and clamps as above. Emoji count as one character, as in Origami since v73.

inputs.name: Text
inputs.description: The text to take characters from.

inputs.name: Start
inputs.description: Which character to begin at, counted from 0. A Start past the last character gives empty text.

inputs.name: Length
inputs.description: How many characters to keep from Start. 0 gives empty text, and more than remain keeps the rest.

inputs.name: Ellipsis
inputs.description: When on, adds "…" after the kept characters if characters after them were cut off.

commonMistakes: The first letter is missing: Start counts from 0, so Start 1 begins at the second character. Set Start to 0.
The output is empty: Start is past the last character, or Length is 0. Lower Start or raise Length.

patches.name: Measure Text
patches.summary: Measures how wide and tall text would be in a given font and size, so shapes can fit around a label.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Measure Text works out the **Size** that **Text** takes up in a given font, using the same layout rules as a Text layer.

- **Font**, **Font Size**, **Weight**, **Letter Spacing**, and **Line Height** match the Text layer properties with the same names. Set them to match the layer you're measuring for.
- **Max Width** is where lines wrap. With 0, text breaks only at line breaks.
- **Size** is the widest line's width and the total height of all lines. Empty text has width 0 and the height of one line.

The result arrives on the same frame. Reading a layer's size instead lags one frame.

## Tips
- Text layers already hug their text when Width Mode is Auto. Measure Text is for other layers that should match the text, such as a badge behind a label or an underline under a tab title.
- Add padding by feeding Size into Add set to Size.
- A font that isn't installed or embedded measures with the fallback font, just as it renders.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly Text Size. Max Width replaces Box Size, Font Name is named Font, Character Spacing is named Letter Spacing, and Weight is new.

inputs.description: The text to measure.

inputs.name: Max Width
inputs.description: The widest a line can be before text wraps, in points. 0 means no limit, so text breaks only at line breaks.

inputs.description: Font family name, the same as the Text layer's Font.

inputs.name: Font Size
inputs.description: Font size in points.

inputs.name: Weight
inputs.description: Font weight, from 100 (thin) to 900 (black).

inputs.name: Letter Spacing
inputs.description: Extra space between characters, in points.

inputs.name: Line Height
inputs.description: Distance between lines in points; 0 uses the font's natural line height.

inputs.name: Paragraph Spacing
inputs.description: Extra space added between paragraphs (text separated by line breaks), in points.

outputs.description: The width of the widest line and the total height, in points, on the current frame.

commonMistakes: The badge is a little too wide or too narrow: Measure Text uses a different font, size, or weight than the Text layer. Set every style port to match the layer.
Long text never wraps: Max Width is 0, which means no limit. Set it to the widest the text may be.
The shape touches the text: Size covers the text alone. Add padding, such as [24, 8] with Add set to Size.

patches.name: Format Date & Time
patches.summary: Turns seconds into readable text: a clock time, a date, a media timestamp like 2:05, or your own % pattern.
patches.docs:
## How it works
Format Date & Time turns **Time**, a number of seconds, into text.

- For clock times and dates, Time is a timestamp: seconds since January 1, 1970, UTC. Device Time and most web APIs give timestamps like this.
- For **Media Time** and **Short Media Time**, Time is a duration, such as a video's current time. 125 seconds shows 02:05 or 2:05, and an hour or more adds hours (1:02:05).
- **Custom** uses **Custom Format**, a pattern of % codes:

| Code | Shows | Code | Shows |
|---|---|---|---|
| %A | Saturday | %a | Sat |
| %B | March | %b | Mar |
| %d | 14 | %Y | 2026 |
| %H | 18 (24-hour) | %I | 06 (12-hour) |
| %M | 30 | %S | 05 |
| %p | PM | %y | 26 |

Put a hyphen after % to drop leading zeros: %-I:%M %p shows 6:30 PM.

Names of months and days are in English. The advanced **Time Zone** port chooses between the device's time zone and UTC.

## Tips
- For a live clock, wire Device Time into Time.
- For elapsed time from Stopwatch, use Media Time.

## Coming from Origami
Formerly Date & Time Formatter. The formats are the same, and Time Zone is new.

inputs.name: Time
inputs.description: Seconds since January 1, 1970 (UTC) for clock times and dates, or a duration in seconds for the Media Time formats.

inputs.name: Format

enumOptions.name: Media Time (02:05)
enumOptions.description: Treats Time as a duration, with zero-padded minutes.

enumOptions.name: Short Media Time (2:05)
enumOptions.description: Treats Time as a duration, without padding the first number.

enumOptions.name: Custom
enumOptions.description: Uses the % codes in Custom Format.

inputs.description: How the text looks: a clock time, a date, a media timestamp, or a custom pattern.

inputs.name: Custom Format
inputs.description: The pattern used when Format is Custom, such as "%B %-d" for March 14. Codes start with %.

inputs.name: Time Zone

enumOptions.name: Device
enumOptions.description: The time zone of the device running the prototype.

enumOptions.name: UTC
enumOptions.description: Coordinated Universal Time, the same everywhere.

inputs.description: Which time zone clock times and dates are shown in; the Media Time formats ignore it.

commonMistakes: A timer shows strange hours or minutes: clock and date formats treat Time as a date in your time zone. Use Media Time for durations, such as Stopwatch's Time.
The date shows January 1, 1970: Time is 0 or a small number. Wire in a timestamp in seconds, such as from Device Time.
The date is thousands of years off, or the text is empty: the timestamp is in milliseconds. Divide it by 1000 before wiring it into Time.
